questions.prompt: What is the default isolation behavior for application target code in modern approachable concurrency?

options.text: Code isolates to the main actor by default unless marked otherwise.
options.explanation: Modern Swift isolates app target code to @MainActor by default. This eliminates boilerplate annotations across user interface files.

options.text: Code executes in an uncoordinated global background thread pool.
options.explanation: Uncoordinated execution was the older default model that required manual main actor annotations everywhere.

options.text: Code runs strictly inside background tasks with low execution priority.
options.explanation: App code does not default to low priority background tasks. It runs on the main actor to protect UI state.

options.text: Code disables compile-time concurrency checking across all modules.
options.explanation: Approachable concurrency maintains strict concurrency checking while simplifying default actor isolation.

questions.prompt: Why did Swift adopt default main actor isolation for application targets?

options.text: Apple removed multi-core processor scheduling support on modern iOS devices.
options.explanation: iOS devices retain full multi-core processing capabilities and background task pools.

options.text: Most app target code touches user interface state and presentation views.
options.explanation: The vast majority of app code touches UI and view models. Defaulting to the main actor removes repetitive annotations.

options.text: The Swift compiler cannot generate asynchronous code on background queues.
options.explanation: The compiler easily generates asynchronous tasks on background cooperative threads.

options.text: Main actor code consumes less physical memory than background thread code.
options.explanation: Actor isolation governs data race safety and execution context rather than raw memory allocation.

questions.prompt: Which keyword allows a synchronous method inside a main-actor-isolated type to opt out of actor isolation?

options.text: override
options.explanation: The override keyword provides a new implementation for a superclass method, not actor detachment.

options.text: convenience
options.explanation: The convenience keyword marks secondary initializers on classes.

options.text: nonisolated
options.explanation: Marking a member nonisolated detaches it from the enclosing type actor isolation.

options.text: dynamic
options.explanation: The dynamic keyword directs member invocation through Objective-C runtime dispatch.

questions.prompt: What happens when an async function on the main actor awaits an off-actor background function?

options.text: The main thread freezes synchronously until the background worker finishes.
options.explanation: Awaiting does not block the thread synchronously. It suspends execution non-blockingly.

options.text: The Swift runtime terminates the process due to an actor boundary mismatch.
options.explanation: Awaiting across actor boundaries is a standard, safe operation supported by Swift Concurrency.

options.text: The background function is forced to execute on the main thread run loop.
options.explanation: Off-actor functions run on background cooperative threads rather than on the main actor.

options.text: Execution hops off the main actor, leaving the UI thread unblocked.
options.explanation: Calling an off-actor function suspends the caller and hops to background worker threads, keeping UI smooth.

questions.prompt: How does approachable concurrency affect shared utility packages and libraries?

options.text: Shared packages still default to non-isolated code to remain versatile.
options.explanation: Default main actor isolation is tailored for app targets. Libraries remain non-isolated to serve multiple platforms.

options.text: Shared packages cannot import the Swift Concurrency standard library module.
options.explanation: Shared packages fully support and import the standard concurrency module.

options.text: Shared packages are converted automatically into UIKit view subclasses.
options.explanation: Library code remains platform-agnostic and is not transformed into UI classes.

options.text: Shared packages refuse to compile unless every function is marked async.
options.explanation: Libraries can freely include both synchronous and asynchronous functions.

questions.prompt: What performance issue happens if you forget to opt out of main actor isolation for heavy JSON decoding?

options.text: The compiler emits a memory leak diagnostic and halts compilation.
options.explanation: Running heavy code on the main actor does not cause memory leaks or compiler errors.

options.text: The main thread blocks during decoding, causing UI hitches and frame drops.
options.explanation: Running heavy work on the main actor monopolizes the main thread run loop, leading to dropped frames.

options.text: The operating system crashes the application with a thread deadlock code.
options.explanation: Executing heavy synchronous work on the main thread causes stutter, not immediate deadlock.

options.text: The JSONDecoder automatically moves the parsing work to GPU hardware.
options.explanation: JSONDecoder does not offload parsing to the GPU. It runs on whatever thread calls it.

questions.prompt: In an approachable concurrency app target, what annotation is needed on a standard SwiftUI ViewModel?

options.text: Every class must still declare explicit @MainActor attribute.
options.explanation: The primary benefit of approachable concurrency is removing the need for explicit @MainActor on app target classes.

options.text: Every class must inherit from a special NSObject actor base class.
options.explanation: Swift view models do not need to inherit from NSObject or an actor base class.

options.text: No explicit annotation is required because app code defaults to @MainActor.
options.explanation: Under approachable concurrency, application classes and structs default to the main actor automatically.

options.text: Every class must use the @preconcurrency attribute on all properties.
options.explanation: @preconcurrency is used during library migration, not on regular app view models.

questions.prompt: What is the role of the @concurrent attribute on an asynchronous function?

options.text: It forces synchronous serial execution on the primary thread run loop.
options.explanation: @concurrent specifies execution on background worker threads, not the main thread.

options.text: It turns the function into an atomic hardware transaction.
options.explanation: @concurrent does not provide hardware transaction memory.

options.text: It disables cooperative task cancellation for the duration of the call.
options.explanation: @concurrent functions remain fully cooperative and support task cancellation.

options.text: It marks the function to run off the main actor on background threads.
options.explanation: @concurrent indicates that the async function should execute on the cooperative background thread pool.

questions.prompt: When can a synchronous function inside a @MainActor class be marked nonisolated?

options.text: When it does not read or mutate mutable actor-isolated stored properties.
options.explanation: A synchronous nonisolated method cannot access mutable actor state because it runs outside the actor protection boundary.

options.text: Only when it modifies at least two private properties simultaneously.
options.explanation: A nonisolated method cannot modify any isolated mutable properties.

options.text: Only when the enclosing class conforms to the Objective-C NSCopying protocol.
options.explanation: Actor isolation does not depend on NSCopying protocol conformance.

options.text: When the method is called exclusively from background Grand Central Dispatch queues.
options.explanation: nonisolated methods can be called from any thread context synchronously.

options.text: Swift 5.5 defaulted to the main actor, while modern Swift defaults to actors.

options.text: Swift 5.5 defaulted to non-isolated, while modern Swift defaults to @MainActor.
options.explanation: Early concurrency required manual main actor annotations. Modern Swift flips the default for app targets.

options.text: Swift 5.5 banned background threads, while modern Swift enables them.
options.explanation: Both versions support background threads through cooperative thread pools.

options.text: There is no difference in default isolation between the two versions.
options.explanation: The isolation default changed significantly from non-isolated to main actor default in app targets.

questions.prompt: What is the recommended mental model for developers using approachable concurrency?

options.text: Run everything on background queues and manually sync to main with locks.
options.explanation: Modern Swift avoids manual locks and dispatch syncs in favor of language-level actors.

options.text: Avoid using async and await in any code that interacts with SwiftUI.
options.explanation: SwiftUI is designed to work seamlessly with async and await.

options.text: Stay on the main actor by default, and opt out for heavy background work.
options.explanation: This mental model keeps UI state safe by default while offloading heavy workloads explicitly.

options.text: Annotate every function with dynamic and nonisolated unconditionally.
options.explanation: Annotating everything nonisolated defeats the safety and ergonomics of default main actor isolation.

questions.prompt: Why can an asynchronous nonisolated function be called from a main-actor view model using await?

options.text: Because await converts the nonisolated function into a main actor function.
options.explanation: Await does not change the isolation of the target function.

options.text: Because the compiler clones the view model instance onto the background thread.
options.explanation: The compiler does not clone view model instances across threads.

options.text: Because nonisolated functions can only return primitive integer literals.
options.explanation: Nonisolated functions can return any Sendable data type.

options.text: Because await provides a safe suspension point across isolation domains.
options.explanation: The await keyword marks an asynchronous suspension point, allowing safe execution across actor boundaries.

options.text: Mutations trigger a fatal thread sanitizer assertion on device launch.
options.explanation: Thread Sanitizer verifies that resuming on the main actor is completely thread-safe.

options.text: Mutations fail silently until the user taps another button on screen.
options.explanation: Resumed execution updates state immediately on the main run loop.

options.text: Mutations require manual calls to NSLock.lock and NSLock.unlock.
options.explanation: Actor isolation replaces manual lock primitives with compiler-enforced guarantees.

questions.prompt: Explain what approachable concurrency changes for application targets in modern Swift, and why Apple chose this default.

rubric.criterion: Explains that application target code isolates to @MainActor by default
Explains that this eliminates repetitive @MainActor annotations on UI code and view models
Notes that most app code touches user interface state and presentation logic

questions.modelAnswer: Approachable concurrency changes the default isolation of application targets to @MainActor. Because most iOS app code directly manipulates user interface state and view models, defaulting to the main actor eliminates repetitive annotations. Developers write standard UI code safely by default and opt out only when performing heavy background work.

questions.prompt: How does a developer move heavy or long-running work off the main actor in an approachable concurrency project?

rubric.criterion: Identifies using nonisolated or @concurrent to opt out of main actor isolation
Explains that calling the background function uses await to hop off the main actor
Mentions that keeping heavy computation off the main thread preserves 60 or 120 frames per second UI smoothness

questions.modelAnswer: Developers move heavy work off the main actor by marking functions as nonisolated or @concurrent. When a main actor caller awaits these functions, execution hops off the main thread to cooperative background threads. This keeps intensive parsing or image calculations from blocking the main run loop, preserving smooth user interface animations.

questions.prompt: Why do shared utility libraries and framework packages still default to non-isolated code rather than @MainActor?

rubric.criterion: Explains that libraries and shared packages must remain platform-agnostic and versatile
Points out that shared packages run in environments without a UI run loop, such as servers or command-line tools
Notes that forcing main actor isolation on libraries would cause unnecessary actor hops on server or background systems

questions.modelAnswer: Shared libraries and framework packages default to non-isolated code because they are designed to be versatile across diverse environments. Unlike client applications, libraries may run on servers, background daemons, or command-line utilities that have no user interface run loop. Defaulting to non-isolated code avoids unnecessary actor hops and keeps shared logic reusable everywhere.

questions.prompt: Describe what restrictions apply when marking a synchronous method inside a @MainActor class as nonisolated.

rubric.criterion: States that the nonisolated method cannot access or mutate mutable actor-isolated stored properties
Explains that synchronous access to isolated mutable state from outside the actor would cause data races
Notes that the method can only access parameters, immutable constants, or its own local variables

questions.modelAnswer: A synchronous nonisolated method inside a @MainActor class cannot read or mutate any mutable actor-isolated stored properties. Allowing direct synchronous access from outside the actor boundary would create data races. Therefore, the method may only operate on passed parameters, immutable constants, or its own internal local variables.

questions.prompt: Compare the developer experience of early Swift Concurrency with modern approachable concurrency in an interview context.
questions.lessonSection: How to answer in the interview

rubric.criterion: Contrasts early Swift non-isolated default with modern @MainActor default for apps
Mentions the reduction in boilerplate annotations and fewer accidental threading mistakes
Explains that developers now follow an opt-out model for heavy background work

questions.modelAnswer: Early Swift Concurrency defaulted all code to non-isolated execution, requiring explicit @MainActor annotations on almost every view model and controller. Approachable concurrency recognizes that app development is UI-centric and defaults application targets to @MainActor. This removes repetitive annotations, lowers cognitive load, and shifts developers to an opt-out model for background work.
